title: From the Ferdinandstrasse to the Treasury: the Acceptance, the Island, and the National Monument
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Third Son on the Ferdinandstrasse

stops.name: Hamburg, born into the banking house
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and city confirmed at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg and de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg. Coordinates are the canonical family pin already carried by the Hamburg birth stop in aby_warburg.journey.json and max_warburg.journey.json, not a verified house address; the dossier's claim of a specific Rotherbaum address could not be confirmed.
stops.campa: On the tenth of August a third son is born in the Warburg house at Hamburg, to Moritz Warburg and Charlotte Oppenheim. Hamburg is a free city with its own senate and its own flag, and merchants who have never taken orders from a king. The family bank on the Ferdinandstrasse is by then seventy years old and runs on a rule nobody has to write down: the sons serve the house, and the house serves the port. Paul Moritz arrives into a settled arithmetic in which the bank already has more sons than it needs, and the surplus will be spent abroad. Aby, the eldest, is two. Max is one.
suggested_refs: The Warburg family houses of the Rotherbaum quarter, Hamburg
sources: aby_warburg.journey.json, stop 'Hamburg, birth into the banking house'

stops.name: Hamburg, the Realgymnasium and no university
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact of Realgymnasium schooling and 1886 graduation (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg); the specific school is not named in any source reached, so the coordinates are Hamburg city centre and the month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He finishes at a Hamburg Realgymnasium, a school built for merchants' sons: modern languages, mathematics, and practical training in the place where a classical curriculum would be. Aby, the eldest, has already traded his birthright in the bank to Max for a promise of unlimited books and is bound for the universities. Paul takes the other road and enters no university at all. What he will know of banking comes out of ledgers and out of the men who keep them, in four cities over the sixteen years after this graduation.
suggested_refs: Hamburg Realgymnasium curricula of the 1880s, modern-language and commercial track
sources: aby_warburg.journey.json, stop 'Hamburg, the bargain with Max'

stops.name: Simon Hauer, the apprenticeship in the merchant quarter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to place, attested as to fact. The apprenticeship at Simon Hauer is confirmed (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg); the firm's address is not, so the coordinates approximate Hamburg's historic merchant district near the Speicherstadt. Month set to follow the spring graduation; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He is apprenticed to Simon Hauer, an import and export house in the merchant quarter by the harbour, and spends three years on invoices, documentary credits, and bills drawn in one currency and paid in another. A bill of exchange is a promise with a date on it. A bank willing to discount it turns that promise into money today. The argument he will make in America for twenty-five years is already on this desk, in the difference between a paper the Bank of England stands behind and a paper nobody stands behind at all. He is eighteen.
suggested_refs: The Hamburg documentary-credit trade of the 1880s and its bill practice

segments.name: Two European Systems, and the Return

stops.name: City of London, the year at Samuel Montagu and Company
stops.date_confidence: attested as to firm and year (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg); the office address inside the City was not verified, so the coordinates are a City-of-London approximation. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Samuel Montagu and Company, bankers and bullion brokers in the City, take him for a year. Here the acceptance market is not a theory. A bill accepted by a first-class London house is as good as cash anywhere on earth, it trades at a known discount, and behind the whole apparatus stands the Bank of England, which in a crisis lends. Warburg is twenty-one and watching a machine that has no American equivalent. He will spend twenty-five years trying to explain to a country of twenty thousand independent banks what it is like to have one. The year at Montagu ends in 1890 and he goes on to Paris.
suggested_refs: The London discount market and the Bank of England's lender-of-last-resort practice, 1889

stops.name: Paris, the Russian Bank for Foreign Trade
stops.date_confidence: attested as to firm and year (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg); the Paris agency's address was not verified. Coordinates are the canonical atlas Paris pin inherited unchanged rather than a located building. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: A year at the Paris agency of the Banque Russe pour le Commerce Etranger adds the continental pattern to the English one. A universal bank lends long, takes equity, and finances governments as readily as it finances merchants; it does not live or die by a discount market. Between London and Paris he has now seen the two European systems that American banking has neither of. The exact address of the agency is lost. Whether the sequence, one year in each house, was his father's plan or his own, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Banque Russe pour le Commerce Etranger and French financing of Russian state credit

stops.name: Ferdinandstrasse 75, into the family bank
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1891 entry (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg). Contradiction left open in the campa: German biographical record has him made Prokurist at M. M. Warburg in 1893, while Encyclopedia.com's chronology instead puts a worldwide study journey in 1893; that page now redirects to a 404 and could not be re-read. Coordinates from de.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._M._Warburg_%26_CO, which places Ferdinandstrasse 75 at 53.5524, 9.9978; the bank moved to that plot in 1868 and rebuilt on it in 1911.
stops.campa: He comes home to the Ferdinandstrasse and takes a desk in M. M. Warburg and Company, the house the family founded in 1798. Max is already there and will hold it for half a century. The German record has Paul made Prokurist, authorized to sign for the firm, in 1893; an American reference work instead sends him around the world that year to study international finance. Both cannot be true, and neither has been decided here. From 1891 he is a Warburg working for Warburgs, in the building the family has occupied since 1868 and will rebuild on the same plot in 1911.
suggested_refs: M. M. Warburg and Company partnership records, Ferdinandstrasse 75, Hamburg
sources: max_warburg.journey.json, stop 'Ferdinandstrasse 75, made a personally liable partner'

stops.name: Ferdinandstrasse 75, made a partner
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1895 partnership (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._M._Warburg_%26_Co.); month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01. The characterisation of a deliberate division of labour between the brothers is a reconstruction drawn from the two brothers' subsequent careers, not from a document.
stops.campa: At twenty-six he is made a partner, in the same year he marries. The house is now run by brothers in the pattern the family prefers: Max in Hamburg holding the German business, Paul available for whatever lies outside it. He keeps the partnership seven years, then hands the German half wholly to Max and takes the American half himself. That is how a Hamburg private bank with no shareholders and no published accounts comes to have a standing partner inside Kuhn, Loeb in lower Manhattan. Neither brother thinks of this as emigration.
suggested_refs: The M. M. Warburg partnership deeds of 1895

segments.name: The Loeb Marriage and the Crossing

stops.name: New York, the wedding his brother crossed for
stops.date_confidence: attested; marriage to Nina Jenny Loeb on 1 October 1895 in New York (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg). The ceremony venue is not named in any source reached; the coordinates are the canonical lower-Manhattan pin already used for this same wedding in aby_warburg.journey.json, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: On the first of October he marries Nina Jenny Loeb, daughter of Solomon Loeb, who founded Kuhn, Loeb and Company in New York thirty years before. The Hamburg house and the New York house are joined by a marriage, which in this family is an ordinary way for capital to travel. He is twenty-seven, and the bride's father is one of the names on the door of the firm he will join seven years from now. Aby crosses the Atlantic for the wedding and, the errand done, keeps going west toward the Smithsonian ethnologists and the Pueblo country.
suggested_refs: The Loeb and Schiff family papers on the Kuhn, Loeb partnership marriages
sources: aby_warburg.journey.json, stop 'New York, his brother Paul's wedding'

stops.name: Hamburg Rathaus, the seat in the Burgerschaft
stops.date_confidence: attested; de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg records him in the Hamburgische Burgerschaft 1900 to 1902, among its first Jewish members. Month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the Rathaus, the chamber's seat, not a location attested for Warburg personally.
stops.campa: For two years he sits in the Hamburgische Burgerschaft, the parliament of the free city, one of its first Jewish members. The seat is real and the German biographical authorities record it plainly. English-language accounts of his life almost never mention it, so that the man who lands in New York in 1902 arrives with no political past that Americans know about, and is described for the rest of his life as a foreign banker who came to Washington. He stood for election in Hamburg first, and won. The rolls of the chamber for 1900 to 1902 carry his name.
suggested_refs: Membership rolls of the Hamburgische Burgerschaft, 1900-1902
sources: max_warburg.journey.json, stop 'Hamburg Rathaus, the seat in the Burgerschaft'

stops.name: Pine Street, the partner's desk at Kuhn, Loeb
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1902 relocation and the partnership (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuhn,_Loeb_%26_Co., which lists him a general partner 1903-1914). Address contradiction noted: the firm was at 27 Pine Street from 1894 and moved to 52 William Street in 1903, so the 1902 arrival belongs to Pine Street. The coordinates given are the William and Pine corner, one block from the earlier door. Month is the autumn given in the dossier; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He settles permanently in New York in the autumn and becomes a general partner at Kuhn, Loeb, then in Pine Street, a firm run by Jacob Schiff and built on railroad securities and foreign government loans. Warburg's side of it is the international one: sterling, marks, the placement of sovereign paper. He speaks English with an accent he never loses, and he finds an American banking system that strikes him, in the word he will use for it in print thirty years later, as cruel. The firm moves the following year to 52 William Street, one block east.
suggested_refs: Kuhn, Loeb and Company partnership records, 27 Pine Street and 52 William Street

stops.name: Fifth Avenue and Twelfth Street, the Institute of Musical Art
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school's founding, founder, funder, date and address (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard_School). Paul and Nina's own patronage is dossier-sourced and was not independently verified, and is a reconstruction here.
stops.campa: The Institute of Musical Art opens in the old Lenox mansion at Fifth Avenue and Twelfth Street, founded by Frank Damrosch and endowed by James Loeb, Nina's brother, who has left the family bank for archaeology and philanthropy and will not come back to it. Paul and Nina are recorded among its patrons. The same partnership profits that finance railroads and sovereign bonds are paying here for a conservatory in a borrowed mansion. James Loeb is at this moment also planning the classical library that will carry his name. The school will become the Juilliard.
suggested_refs: The Loeb Classical Library, endowed by James Loeb, brother-in-law to Paul Warburg

stops.name: New York, the article in the Times
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The essay 'Defects and Needs of Our Banking System' in the New York Times is attested in the dossier chronology and in Federal Reserve founding summaries, but the 1907 text itself was not fetched in this pass and the exact publication day is not pinned; month and day defaulted to 01. The Medici comparison reaches this file through the dossier's report of that article, not through the article. Coordinates are a Wall Street placeholder shared with several New York stops here.
stops.campa: Warburg publishes 'Defects and Needs of Our Banking System' in the New York Times, his first American argument in public. The country, he writes, has reached roughly the stage of banking development that Europe reached in the time of the Medici, when Cosimo de' Medici's bank kept branches in half the cities of the continent and no state kept a reserve for anybody. Thousands of independent banks sit on their own cash, and nothing turns good commercial paper into money on demand. He will go on making that argument in print and in committee rooms until 1913.
suggested_refs: Paul M. Warburg, 'Defects and Needs of Our Banking System,' New York Times, 1907
cosimo_de_medici.journey.json, on the branch structure of the Medici bank
sources: dossier chronology, after Federal Reserve History summaries

stops.name: Wall Street, the panic
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Panic of 1907 occurred and that clearing-house cooperation and J. P. Morgan's private coordination contained it; month set to October, day defaulted to 01, because the pool fixes only the year. The quote is Warburg's own retrospective account written in 1930, not a contemporaneous statement.
stops.campa: In October the Knickerbocker Trust suspends and the panic runs through New York. Banks that are solvent cannot pay, because paying means calling in loans from other banks that are also solvent and also cannot pay. J. P. Morgan holds the presidents of the trust companies in his library until they agree to a rescue, and the clearing houses issue their own scrip because there is no other elastic currency to issue. The private coordination works. Warburg draws from that success the conclusion nobody else in the city draws from it.
stops.quote: As already mentioned, without a central reserve organization and without an elastic note issue, one bank could only strengthen itself by weakening another, and any attempt to call in funds from a debtor would only throw him into desperate confusion and set in motion a chain of further embarrassments and insolvencies.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (New York: Macmillan, 1930), vol. I, p. 21, on the Panic of 1907. Verified against the archive.org full text, item federalreservesy0001paul.
suggested_refs: The Knickerbocker Trust suspension and the clearing-house certificates of October 1907
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, p. 21, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: New York, a plan for a modified central bank
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pamphlet is dated 12 November 1907 and is reprinted by Warburg himself in his 1930 volume, where the quote was verified verbatim against the archive.org text. Coordinates are the shared Wall Street placeholder.
stops.campa: Five weeks after the worst of it he publishes a plan for a modified central bank, the first of the schemes he will revise for six years. The word central is the difficulty and he knows it: an American reader hears in it Nicholas Biddle, Andrew Jackson, and a monopoly of money held in one city. So he modifies, and keeps modifying, and the modifications are the political history of the Federal Reserve in miniature. The problem he has set himself is a reserve that behaves like one bank while consisting of many, owned by bankers and governed in part by the state.
stops.quote: We need some centralized power to protect us against others and to protect us from ourselves, some power able to provide for the legitimate needs of the country and able at the same time to apply the brakes when the car is moving too fast.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, 'A Plan for a Modified Central Bank,' 12 November 1907, reprinted in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, p. 23.
suggested_refs: The Second Bank of the United States and the Jacksonian bank war, the memory Warburg is writing against
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, p. 23, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: New York, the letter to Senator Aldrich
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated New York, 31 December 1907, and is printed as Appendix Two of Warburg's own 1930 volume, where both quoted passages were verified verbatim against the archive.org text. Coordinates are the shared Wall Street placeholder.
stops.campa: On the last day of the year he writes to Nelson Aldrich, Republican senator from Rhode Island, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, father-in-law to a Rockefeller, and the most powerful man in American monetary legislation. Aldrich has outlined a scheme for an additional currency backed by clearing-house certificates. Warburg answers that emergency currency treats a symptom, and that what the autumn exposed was decentralization itself. The letter opens a correspondence between an immigrant banker and a senator who has, at this date, no particular reason to answer it.
stops.quote: Did not the last panic show that we are suffering from too much decentralization of our banking system and from the absolute impossibility of securing any concerted action as to the free use of our reserves, instead of competitive hoarding of currency by the financial institutions?
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, 'Letter to Senator Aldrich,' New York, 31 December 1907, printed as Appendix Two in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, pp. 555-556.
suggested_refs: The Aldrich-Vreeland Act of 1908, the emergency-currency answer Warburg argued against
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, Appendix Two, pp. 555-556, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: Washington, The Discount System in Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested; the archive.org catalogue record gives 'The discount system in Europe,' Paul Moritz Warburg and the United States National Monetary Commission, 1910. FRASER returns 403 to automated fetch, so archive.org is the citation of record. Month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are Washington, the Commission's seat, not a located building.
stops.campa: The Aldrich-Vreeland Act has created a National Monetary Commission and sent it to Europe; Warburg becomes its explainer at home. The Government Printing Office publishes his study of the European discount system for the Commission, and in the same year he circulates a plan for a United Reserve Bank of the United States. The technical case and the political case have to be made together, because the objection to a reserve bank is never that the mechanism will not work. The objection is that it will work for somebody in particular.
stops.quote: A central reserve bank properly organized is not an oligarchic but a democratic institution; it would mean safety for all, hardship for none.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, 'A United Reserve Bank of the United States' (1910), reprinted in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, p. 54.
suggested_refs: Publications of the National Monetary Commission, 1910-1912, Government Printing Office
sources: archive.org catalogue, 'The discount system in Europe' (1910)
Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, p. 54

stops.name: Hoboken Terminal, the private car with the blinds down
stops.date_confidence: attested; the departure from Hoboken on the evening of 22 November 1910 and the first-names-only cover are confirmed at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jekyll_Island_Club. Arthur Shelton is named as Aldrich's secretary in the same body of sources; the attendance of Benjamin Strong and Charles D. Norton is disputed in the scholarly literature and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: On the evening of the twenty-second of November a private railroad car waits at the Hoboken terminal with its blinds down. Aldrich is one of the party; Warburg is another; with them are Davison of Morgan's, Vanderlip of National City, Andrew from the Treasury, and Aldrich's secretary Shelton. Any bill carrying those six names would have died in committee, so the secrecy is not decoration. The men board separately, having agreed to use first names only so that porters and trainmen cannot piece the party together, and to tell anyone who asks that they are going duck shooting.
suggested_refs: Frank A. Vanderlip's later account of the Hoboken departure and the duck-shooting cover story
sources: Federal Reserve History, essay on the Jekyll Island conference

stops.name: Jekyll Island Club, first names only
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place, secrecy, and the core participants; the exact day of arrival is not fixed in the sources reached and is set here to follow the 22 November departure. Coordinates are the Jekyll Island Club Historic District as given by its Wikipedia article, inherited from the same pin in the verification pass.
stops.campa: For about nine days on a Georgia sea island, in a club whose kitchen has been told to expect a hunting party, they write the outline of a National Reserve Association. Warburg supplies the European mechanics: acceptances, a discount rate, reserves pooled instead of hoarded, a note that is elastic because it is issued against real commercial paper. The others supply what will pass. They carry off the island a draft no Democrat will vote for. Whether Benjamin Strong and Charles Norton were also there is disputed among historians and is not settled here.
suggested_refs: The Jekyll Island Club Historic District, Georgia
G. Edward Griffin, The Creature from Jekyll Island (1994), the leading conspiracist account of this week, and Peter Conti-Brown's assessment of it

stops.name: New York, the oath of citizenship
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of naturalization (Encyclopedia.com chronology, corroborated by standard biographical summaries); month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the canonical lower-Manhattan pin, not a located courthouse. The quote is from his 1918 letter to Wilson, quoting the oath back seven years later, and is placed here where the oath itself was sworn.
stops.campa: He takes the oath of citizenship at forty-two, nine years after settling in New York and one year after Jekyll Island. He has already drafted the plan for an American central reserve organization; he becomes an American afterwards. That sequence will be held against him for the rest of his life and past the end of it. Seven years later, defending himself to a president in wartime, he goes back to the words of the oath itself and to what he understood himself to be doing on the day he said them.
stops.quote: I did not swear that "I absolutely and entirely renounce and abjure all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign potentate, and particularly to Wilhelm II, Emperor of Germany," etc. until I was quite certain that I was willing and anxious to cast my lot unqualifiedly and without reserve with the country of my adoption and to defend its aims and its ideals.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, 'Letter to President Wilson,' Washington, 27 May 1918, printed as Appendix Thirty-Two in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, p. 802.
suggested_refs: United States naturalization oath, form of 1906
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, Appendix Thirty-Two, p. 802

stops.name: The Capitol, the Commission's report
stops.date_confidence: attested; the National Monetary Commission submitted its report and a draft bill of fifty-nine sections on 9 January 1912 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act). Contradiction flagged: the dossier chronology gave 8 January, one day early, and is not followed here.
stops.campa: The National Monetary Commission delivers its final report and a draft bill of fifty-nine sections to Congress. The Aldrich Plan is now a public document with a Republican senator's name on it, in an election year. Wilson wins. The Democrats take Congress. The plan is politically dead within the year of its printing, and its mechanics are going to be enacted inside two years by the men who campaigned against them, under another name and with a public board set over them. The platform they campaigned on declares against 'the Aldrich plan or a central bank.'
suggested_refs: Report of the National Monetary Commission, 9 January 1912
The 1912 Democratic Party platform, plank on the Aldrich plan

stops.name: New York, the draft made to fit a Democratic platform
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Warburg's advisory work at Henry Morgenthau's request, and the date, come from the dossier chronology as reflected in Federal Reserve founding histories; no primary correspondence was reached in this pass. Coordinates are the shared Wall Street placeholder.
stops.campa: At Henry Morgenthau's request Warburg prepares a version of the reserve plan that a Democratic administration could sign, moving the government appointments up and the bankers' control down. He is not in the room where the Glass bill is drafted and he holds no office in the incoming government. He is the man both sides send drafts to. The tradition that he wrote the Federal Reserve Act grows up later and is false. What the record shows in December 1912 is a private banker with no constituency and no vote, correcting other men's drafts at their invitation, in a vocabulary everybody ends up using.
suggested_refs: The Glass-Owen bill drafting record, House and Senate committee papers, 1913
sources: dossier chronology, after Federal Reserve founding histories

stops.name: The Capitol, before the House Banking Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and substance, but through Warburg's own 1930 recollection of his testimony rather than through the hearing transcript, which was not reached. Coordinates are the Capitol, where the committee sat.
stops.campa: He appears before the House Committee on Banking and Currency and argues for something no bankers' association has asked for: that the government should appoint a little more than half the members of the central board. Coming from a Kuhn, Loeb partner this concedes the one thing Wall Street most wants kept, and it is the concession that makes the system politically possible. Carter Glass's bill, when it emerges, puts the Secretary of the Treasury and the Comptroller of the Currency on the board as members by right of office.
stops.quote: When I appeared before the House Committee on January 7th, 1913, I expressed the view that in order to bring about a well balanced control of the System it would be advisable to empower the government to appoint a little more than one-half of the members of the board of the central office.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, p. 55, summarising his own testimony of 7 January 1913.
suggested_refs: Hearings of the House Committee on Banking and Currency on banking and currency reform, January 1913
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, p. 55, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: The White House, the Act signed
stops.date_confidence: attested; the signing date is fixed in federal statute history, Federal Reserve Act, 38 Stat. 251. Coordinates are the White House. Warburg's own presence or absence at the signing is not established by anything reached and is not asserted.
stops.campa: Two days before Christmas, Wilson signs the Federal Reserve Act. Twelve regional reserve banks owned by their member banks; a board in Washington appointed by the President; notes issued against gold and commercial paper; a discount window that lends on real bills. Almost every mechanism in it Warburg has been arguing for since 1907. Almost every political arrangement in it was written by men working against the plan he put his name to on the island. The word central appears nowhere in the title.
suggested_refs: Federal Reserve Act, 23 December 1913, 38 Stat. 251

stops.name: Washington, before the Reserve Bank Organization Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and substance; Warburg's testimony is printed as Appendix Twenty-Eight of his 1930 volume and headed 'in January, 1914,' with no day given, so the day is defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the Treasury Building at 1500 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury_Building_(Washington,_D.C.); the dossier's earlier pin for these Washington stops fell on the Ellipse and is not used.
stops.campa: Before the Reserve Bank Organization Committee, which must decide how many reserve districts there will be and which cities get them, Warburg testifies on the arithmetic of concentration. National bank capital and surplus are not spread evenly across the map, and a division pretending otherwise will produce reserve banks too small to matter in a crisis. He will spend his four years on the Board arguing that the districts have to be made to act as one. In April the Committee settles on twelve, more than he thinks defensible.
stops.quote: The little corner on the map embracing New York, New England, and Pennsylvania would contain $800,000,000 of national bank capital and surplus, as compared to a total of the United States of $1,700,000,000
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, 'Testimony Before the Reserve Bank Organization Committee in January, 1914,' printed as Appendix Twenty-Eight in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, p. 759.
suggested_refs: Decision of the Reserve Bank Organization Committee, April 1914, establishing the twelve districts
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, Appendix Twenty-Eight, p. 759, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: The Capitol, Senator Bristow's day and a half
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The hostility of the confirmation hearing, Bristow's questioning, and Warburg's denial of any Rothschild agency come from the dossier chronology and from Time's later recollection of the fight; federalreservehistory.org returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch and the Senate hearing record itself was not reached, so the 1 and 3 August dates are unconfirmed.
stops.campa: Wilson has named him to the first Federal Reserve Board and the Senate Banking Committee will not simply confirm him. Senator Joseph Bristow of Kansas questions him across roughly a day and a half about Kuhn, Loeb, about interlocking directorates, about whether he is an agent of the Rothschilds. Warburg denies the agency. He has already resigned from Kuhn, Loeb and from his other directorships, Wells Fargo among them, to qualify under conflict rules he helped write. It does not shorten the questioning.
suggested_refs: Senate Banking and Currency Committee, confirmation proceedings on the first Federal Reserve Board, August 1914
sources: Time, 'Business & Finance: Warburg Warns,' 18 March 1929, time.com/archive/6743142

stops.name: The Treasury Building, sworn in at forty-six
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of taking office (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg), which is also his forty-sixth birthday. The claim that the Board's first offices were rooms inside the Treasury is general institutional history and was not confirmed by anything fetched; treat it as reconstruction. Coordinates are the Treasury Building.
stops.campa: He is confirmed and takes his seat on the first Federal Reserve Board on the tenth of August, his forty-sixth birthday. Europe went to war eleven days ago, so the system built to end American panics is opening for business in the middle of a world one. The Board has no building. It works out of rooms in the Treasury on Pennsylvania Avenue, with the Secretary of the Treasury sitting as its chairman by right of office, and no settled idea yet of whether it governs the twelve reserve banks or merely watches them.
suggested_refs: The Federal Reserve Board's first quarters in the Treasury Building, 1914-1937

stops.name: Washington, the twelve banks open
stops.date_confidence: attested; 16 November 1914 is the standard opening date of the twelve Federal Reserve Banks across federal and historical sources. Coordinates are the Board's Treasury quarters, not any one reserve bank; the twelve opened in twelve cities on the same day.
stops.campa: The twelve Federal Reserve Banks open for business, four months after the outbreak of war closed the New York Stock Exchange and drove gold out of the country. There is no transition period. Reserve requirements change, the Aldrich-Vreeland emergency currency is retired, and a discount window that has existed on paper for eleven months has to begin actually lending. The acceptance market Warburg came to America carrying has to be built from nothing, because in 1914 there is no American bill of exchange trading anywhere in the world.
suggested_refs: Federal Reserve System opening statements, 16 November 1914

stops.name: Washington, made vice governor
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg gives him vice governor from 10 August 1916, again his birthday. The substance of his gold-concentration argument is reconstruction from the dossier and general Federal Reserve histories. Coordinates are the Treasury Building.
stops.campa: On his forty-eighth birthday Wilson designates him vice governor of the Board. The office gives him a place to press the argument he most wants to make from inside: that the twelve banks must pool their gold rather than each sit on its own, and that a rate set in New York and a rate set in Dallas cannot be allowed to drift apart if the system is to mean anything. Against him stands the plain reading of the Act, which deliberately made twelve banks and not one. The dispute is not settled in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: The interdistrict gold settlement fund and the early rate-uniformity dispute, 1915-1920

stops.name: Kansas City, the reserve problem before the bankers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The address 'The Reserve Problem and the Future of the Federal Reserve System' survives in the dossier bibliography as a title and a date only; the convention hall was not identified, so the coordinates are downtown Kansas City.
stops.campa: He goes to Kansas City to address the American Bankers Association on the reserve problem and the future of the Federal Reserve System. The bankers in that hall own the reserve banks and elect six of the nine directors of each. They are the constituency he has to persuade that concentration of reserves is not confiscation of reserves, and he makes this speech, in different rooms and different cities, for twenty years. The text survives in the bibliographies as a title and a date. The hall it was given in is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the American Bankers Association convention, Kansas City, 1916
sources: dossier bibliography entry, title and date only

stops.name: Washington, the letter to Wilson
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated Washington, 27 May 1918, and Warburg printed it himself as Appendix Thirty-Two of his 1930 volume, where the quote was verified verbatim against the archive.org text. The correction of record: the two brothers in Germany are Max and Fritz at the Ferdinandstrasse. Felix had emigrated, naturalised, and become a Kuhn, Loeb partner, and is not one of the two.
stops.campa: With the country at war against Germany, Warburg's birth and his brothers in Hamburg become a public matter. He writes to Wilson on the twenty-seventh of May asking that his name not be resubmitted for reappointment if a fight over it would damage the system he helped build, and setting down for the record what he takes himself to be. Max and Fritz are at the Ferdinandstrasse serving Germany with everything they have, exactly as he says. Felix is in New York, a Kuhn, Loeb partner and an American, and is not one of the two.
stops.quote: These are sad times. For all of us they bring sad duties, doubly hard, indeed, for men of my extraction. But, though, as in the Civil War, brother must fight brother, each must follow the straight path of duty, and in this spirit I have endeavored to serve during the four years that it has been my privilege to be a member of the Federal Reserve Board.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, 'Letter to President Wilson,' Washington, 27 May 1918, printed as Appendix Thirty-Two in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, pp. 802-803.
suggested_refs: Warburg-Wilson correspondence, May 1918, Appendix Thirty-Two of the 1930 volume
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, Appendix Thirty-Two, pp. 802-803, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: Washington, the term expires
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date; Board service ended 9 August 1918 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg). Contradiction flagged and not resolved: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warburg_family calls the same event a resignation in August 1918, while the Board membership tables record a four-year term running to its end. This file asserts neither reading.
stops.campa: His four-year term ends on the ninth of August, the day before his fiftieth birthday, and he leaves the Federal Reserve Board. Whether this was a resignation or an expiry is not agreed. The membership tables record a term run to its end; a family account calls it a resignation. His own letter of May, asking only that his name not be resubmitted if a fight would damage the system, sits between the two readings and closes neither. He is fifty tomorrow. He holds no federal office again, and watches the institution he argued into being from New York for fourteen years.
suggested_refs: Federal Reserve Board membership tables, 1914-1918

stops.name: New York, the American Acceptance Council
stops.date_confidence: attested for founding and chairmanship in 1919 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg). Month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01. The Council's office address was not identified; coordinates are the shared Wall Street placeholder.
stops.campa: Out of office, he founds the American Acceptance Council and chairs its executive committee. The purpose is narrow and entirely his own: to make the bankers' acceptance an ordinary American instrument, standard in form and traded in a real market, so that a New York merchant financing a cargo need not route the paper through London. This is the piece of the London machinery he has been trying to import since 1902. It cannot be legislated into existence. It has to be sold, bank by bank, to men who have never written one.
suggested_refs: Acceptance Bulletin of the American Acceptance Council, 1919-1930

stops.name: Amsterdam, the bankers who met without governments
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and thin. The Amsterdam meetings with Vissering, Fred I. Kent, Raphael-Georges Levy and Keynes are asserted only in the dossier; no primary or secondary source for them was reached, and john_maynard_keynes.journey.json has no Amsterdam stop and does not mention Warburg. Keynes's June 1919 Treasury resignation and his writing of The Economic Consequences of the Peace that autumn are independently attested and are the only firm part of the setting. Coordinates are Amsterdam city centre; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He crosses to Amsterdam in the autumn for private meetings of bankers from countries that were at war with each other eleven months ago. Gerard Vissering of the Netherlands Bank is there, and Fred Kent, and Raphael-Georges Levy, and John Maynard Keynes, who resigned from the British Treasury delegation at Versailles in June in disgust and is at this moment writing the book that will make him famous. No government is represented at the table. What comes out of these rooms feeds into the Brussels financial conference the following year.
suggested_refs: The Brussels International Financial Conference, 1920
john_maynard_keynes.journey.json, on the 1919 Treasury resignation and The Economic Consequences of the Peace

stops.name: New York, the International Acceptance Bank
stops.date_confidence: attested for founding and chairmanship in 1921 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg, corroborated by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency obituary). Month and day not recorded and defaulted to 01; the bank's office address was not identified, so the coordinates are the shared Wall Street placeholder.
stops.campa: He organizes the International Acceptance Bank in New York and takes the chairmanship. It is built for one purpose, to finance foreign trade and European reconstruction with dollar acceptances, which is to say to do out of New York what the City of London did before 1914 and can no longer afford to do. The war has moved the world's creditor position across the Atlantic and left the instruments behind on the other side. Warburg spends the twenties supplying the instruments. He is fifty-two, and he is still signing this bank's annual reports as its chairman in 1929.
suggested_refs: International Acceptance Bank annual reports, 1921-1931
sources: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Death of Paul M. Warburg,' jta.org/archive

stops.name: Washington, the Federal Advisory Council
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Encyclopedia.com's chronology has him on the Advisory Council through 1926 and presiding from 1924, but that page now redirects to a 404 and could not be re-read, and no membership roster was reached. Month set to 02 only to order the segment after the bank's founding; the actual month is unknown. Coordinates are the Board's Washington quarters.
stops.campa: He returns to the system as a private banker rather than an officer, taking the New York district's seat on the Federal Advisory Council, the body of twelve bankers the Act created to advise a Board it cannot instruct. He holds the seat through 1926 and presides over the council from 1924. It is an odd afterlife for a founder, and he uses it the way he used the New York Times in 1907, as a place to be on the record: quarterly meetings in Washington, formal recommendations, no vote on anything.
suggested_refs: Minutes of the Federal Advisory Council, 1921-1926
sources: Encyclopedia.com chronology, 'Paul Moritz Warburg' (page now returns 404)

stops.name: New York, the Council on Foreign Relations incorporated
stops.date_confidence: attested; incorporation on 29 July 1921 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Foreign_Relations) and Warburg as a director 1921-1932 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg). The Council had no premises of its own until Harold Pratt House in 1945, so the coordinates are the canonical lower-Manhattan pin and not a building.
stops.campa: The Council on Foreign Relations is incorporated in New York on the twenty-ninth of July, an association of bankers, lawyers and academics formed because the Senate has rejected the League and the men who wanted it intend to go on talking anyway. Warburg is among its directors and stays one until he dies. Nearly all of his institutional life after 1918 takes this form, an office held in a body with no premises. The Council has no building of its own for another twenty-four years. It meets in members' offices and in clubs.
suggested_refs: Council on Foreign Relations founding records, 1921

stops.name: Jackson Place, the Institute of Economics
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to Warburg's trusteeship, which rests on the dossier alone. The 8 December 1927 consolidation of the Institute of Economics, the Institute for Government Research and the Robert Brookings Graduate School into the Brookings Institution is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookings_Institution). The 1922 Institute address was not confirmed; Jackson Place is used as the approximate early Brookings-lineage location. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He becomes a trustee of the Institute of Economics on Jackson Place, a research body founded to study public questions with nobody's money riding on the answers. He is fifty-four, four years out of federal office, and the rest of his public work will be done from bodies like this one, acceptance councils and research institutes, none of them government. On the eighth of December 1927 the Institute consolidates with the Institute for Government Research and the Robert Brookings Graduate School into the Brookings Institution. He continues as a trustee of the merged body.
suggested_refs: Brookings Institution founding records, consolidation of 8 December 1927

stops.name: Pasadena, the first draft
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the year and the rest period, which come from the dossier; the fact that the first draft was prepared at Pasadena is attested by the first sentence of Warburg's own Preface, verified in the archive.org text. No hotel or residence was identified, so the coordinates are Pasadena city centre. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes a rest in Pasadena, in poor health, and begins the first draft of the book. It will run to two volumes, part memoir and part documentary history, printing his own letters and plans and testimony from 1907 forward so that nobody has to take his word for any of it. He is writing against two charges at once: that the Federal Reserve is a private conspiracy, and that it is a bureaucratic accident. When he comes to write the Preface, its first sentence says the first draft was prepared at Pasadena.
stops.quote: Considerations such as these were uppermost in my mind when I reached the conclusion that it was my duty to venture upon the difficult and in many respects unwelcome task of writing this book.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, Introduction, p. 7.
suggested_refs: The Paul Moritz Warburg Papers, Yale University Library, the manuscript base of the 1930 volumes
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, Preface p. ix and Introduction p. 7, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: New York, the annual report of March 1929
stops.date_confidence: attested as to text and date through Warburg's own reprint: Appendix Thirty-Seven of the 1930 volume is headed 'Remarks of the Author as Chairman of International Acceptance Bank, Inc., made in his Annual Report March 7, 1929,' verified in the archive.org text. Contradiction flagged: the dossier chronology dated the same report 9 March. Time's coverage of 18 March 1929 carries 'incorporated stock pools' and 'grotesquely impotent and out of line' but gives no date and does not contain the 'orgies' passage, which reaches general circulation through Galbraith rather than through Time.
stops.campa: In the annual report of the International Acceptance Bank he tells his shareholders that the stock market has become a debauch, that the investment trusts are incorporated stock pools, and that the Federal Reserve's rate is grotesquely impotent and out of line. He is warning seven months ahead about the machine he spent his life building, the one he promised in 1907 would apply the brakes when the car was moving too fast. The press picks it up within days. The Street answers that Warburg is sandbagging American prosperity for reasons of his own.
stops.quote: History, which has a painful way of repeating itself, has taught mankind that speculative overexpansion invariably ends in overcontraction and distress. If a stock-exchange debauch is quickly arrested by prompt and determined action, it is not too much to hope that a shrinkage of inflated stock prices may be brought about without seriously affecting the wider circle of general business. If orgies of unrestrained speculation are permitted to spread too far, however, the ultimate collapse is certain not only to affect the speculators themselves, but also to bring about a general depression involving the entire country.
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, remarks as chairman of the International Acceptance Bank in his annual report of 7 March 1929, printed as Appendix Thirty-Seven in The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (1930), vol. I, p. 824.
suggested_refs: Time, 'Business & Finance: Warburg Warns,' 18 March 1929
John Kenneth Galbraith, The Great Crash 1929, on the reception of Warburg's March warning
sources: Warburg, The Federal Reserve System (1930), vol. I, Appendix Thirty-Seven, p. 824, archive.org federalreservesy0001paul

stops.name: New York, the news from Hamburg
stops.date_confidence: attested for Aby Warburg's death of a heart attack in Hamburg on 26 October 1929 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aby_Warburg). Paul's own presence in New York on that day is inferred, not attested, and the coordinates are a New York placeholder. His financial support of Aby's library is a dossier claim that could not be independently verified and is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: Aby dies of a heart attack in Hamburg on the twenty-sixth of October, two days after Black Thursday and three before Black Tuesday, at sixty-three. He leaves the library on the Heilwigstrasse that family money built and that Paul is said to have helped fund, sixty thousand volumes shelved not by subject but along the paths a question takes through them. In New York the exchange is doing what Paul told it in March it would do. The cable reaches him in the middle of it.
suggested_refs: The Kulturwissenschaftliche Bibliothek Warburg, Heilwigstrasse 116, Hamburg
sources: dossier claim of Paul's contribution to the library, unverified

stops.name: New York, the two volumes
stops.date_confidence: attested for publisher, city, year and two-volume form, confirmed through the Arno Press 1975 reprint record at archive.org/details/federalreservesy0000warb, which is explicitly a reprint of the Macmillan edition. The dossier's April month is not supported by anything reached and is dropped; month and day defaulted to 01. The quoted 'national monument' passage is verified verbatim in the archive.org full text at vol. I, Introduction, p. 10, not in the Preface as the dossier had it.
stops.campa: Macmillan publishes The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth in two volumes, the second of them the essays he has written since 1906. The appendices in the first print the documents themselves, the letters and plans and testimony, so that a reader can check the argument against paper. He is sixty-one, the system is sixteen, and the country is a year into the collapse the system was built to prevent. He claims no authorship of it. He asks instead to be read as one mason among many on a cathedral.
stops.quote: the Reserve System is the product of the labors of many minds, that it is the common property and ward of all the people... In order to be accorded its proper place, the Reserve System must be looked upon as a national monument, like the old cathedrals of Europe, which were the work of many generations and of many masters
stops.quote_source: Paul M. Warburg, The Federal Reserve System: Its Origin and Growth (New York: Macmillan, 1930), vol. I, Introduction, p. 10. The ellipsis elides 'and that all must feel an equal degree of concern and responsibility for its welfare.'
suggested_refs: Arno Press reprint of 1975, archive.org/details/federalreservesy0000warb

stops.name: New York, gravely ill
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency dispatch of 15 January 1932 reporting him seriously ill and his condition 'causing extreme anxiety'; the dispatch's recollection of Henry Ford's earlier attacks is carried in the dossier as a reconstruction and was not re-read this pass. The house address is not given in any source reached, so the coordinates are an Upper East Side placeholder rather than a verified residence.
stops.campa: The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports that Paul M. Warburg is seriously ill with pneumonia at his home in New York and that his condition is causing extreme anxiety. The dispatch recalls, as such dispatches then did, that Henry Ford's Dearborn Independent had spent the twenties naming him in print as a foreign hand working inside American finance, and that the accusation had never been retracted so much as dropped. He is sixty-three, and he suffered a slight stroke a month ago. The last two years he has spent watching the European banking system fail and the German half of his family's house go down with it.
suggested_refs: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Mr. Paul M. Warburg Seriously Ill,' 15 January 1932

stops.name: New York, death at home
stops.date_confidence: attested; death on 24 January 1932 in New York City, of pneumonia following a slight stroke about a month earlier, confirmed independently at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg and de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency dispatch of 26 January is the report date, not the death date; earlier dossier hedging to 'mid-to-late January' is unnecessary and is not followed. Coordinates remain the unverified Upper East Side placeholder.
stops.campa: He dies at home in New York on Sunday the twenty-fourth of January, of pneumonia following the stroke, aged sixty-three. He has outlived the Aldrich Plan, the first Board, and the fight over whether a foreign-born banker could sit on it, and his exact address is given in none of the reports. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's dispatch two days later attributes the collapse partly to overexertion connected with the European economic crisis, and names his surviving brothers: Felix in New York, Max in Hamburg.
suggested_refs: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Death of Paul M. Warburg,' 26 January 1932, jta.org/archive

stops.name: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, the grave on the Hudson
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial place: Warburg appears in the notable-burials list at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery. The burial date is not attested anywhere reached and is set here only to follow the 24 January death. Coordinates corrected to the cemetery's own figures, 41 deg 5' 48" N, 73 deg 51' 41" W; three different pairs for this cemetery circulated in the research pool and all are reconciled to these.
stops.campa: He is buried at Sleepy Hollow in Westchester, above the river, among the Rockefellers and a good part of the New York money of his century. Fourteen years later Max, driven out of Hamburg by the Reich and naturalised American at seventy-seven, is buried in the same ground, so that the two brothers who divided the family bank into a German half and an American half end within a few hundred yards of each other on the Hudson. Aby, who never crossed for good, died in Hamburg two years and three months before. No plot number for Paul is recorded.
suggested_refs: Sleepy Hollow Cemetery notable burials, Westchester County, New York
sources: max_warburg.journey.json, stop 'Sleepy Hollow, the grave the reference works do not record'
